lead: Every Monday Carlos opens the agent's dashboard and says: "look how it's climbing!" It really is climbing. But the dashboard started counting the day the agent came on board, and it only shows volume. Without the before, any rise looks like a win, and any redesign has no proof. In this lesson you pick three indicators with a denominator and record today's value before you change anything.
objetivo: define 3 indicators with a numerator, a denominator, and today's value, observed or marked as a hypothesis, before changing the process.

aprende.t: Why volume goes up without proving anything
Write an indicator as a fraction, with a period and a source
Mark what is observed and what is a hypothesis
A target with a deadline and the guardrail for what can't get worse

hero_alt: The business owner and the sales manager look at a printed bar chart and a line chart on the laptop; she points to the start of the chart.

secoes.sub: From the question to the guardrail. Tap each part.

nos.detalhe: Start with the business question, not the number you happen to have. "Does the order become an invoice faster and with less rework?" leads to different indicators than "does the agent serve a lot of people?".

What you count divided by the universe you count in. "Orders returned by billing" on its own says nothing; divided by "orders that reached billing this week," it does. Without a denominator, the number grows along with the volume.
Week, month, four weeks. And the source: counted in a system, observed in tracked cases, or stated by someone. Always compare similar periods (the end of the month isn't the start).

The value before any change. If it hasn't been counted yet, it goes in as a hypothesis, with the date it will become observed. A marked hypothesis is honesty; a stated number treated as measured is a trap.

nos.sub: where to, and without making what worse
nos.detalhe: A target with a value and a deadline. And a guardrail: what can't get worse while you chase the target (invoice errors, discounts outside policy, complaints). Improving one number by wrecking another is not improvement.

secoes.legenda: Indicator rules from the Gestoria method (INEMA): always period, population, denominator, and source; test, pilot, and production kept separate.

secoes.titulo: From the dashboard that climbs to the baseline
secoes.sub: The dashboard numbers come from the lab (fictional study company). Open the piece and check.

texto: Hora's dashboard shows conversations rising from 702 (week of 09/01) to 901 (week of 10/13), and closed orders from 141 to 168. The collection started the same day the agent came on board. There is no before and no comparison.
Satisfaction comes from a star-rating button that about 6% of customers answer. An average of those who answered doesn't speak for the other 94%.

exemplo.rot: The math the dashboard doesn't do
exemplo.texto: Orders ÷ conversations: 141 ÷ 702 = 20.1% on 09/01; 168 ÷ 901 = 18.6% on 10/13. Volume went up and conversion went down. "Climbing" doesn't prove the agent helped.

texto: For the order-to-invoice process, three questions are enough: how long it takes, how much comes back, how much people's work it uses. Each one becomes a fraction with a period and a source.

Time is measured by the median, not the average: one order stuck for three days pulls the average up and hides the normal. Add the typical worst case (the p95) so you don't lose sight of the stuck ones.

exemplo.texto: Time from confirmed order to invoice (median and p95 of the orders invoiced in the week). Orders returned ÷ orders that reached billing. People's minutes ÷ orders invoiced.

texto: The five cases in lesson 3 give you a clue, not the baseline. The baseline comes from four weeks counted in the systems, before any change. Until then, today's value goes in marked as a hypothesis, with the date it becomes observed.
Freed-up people time is not saved money either: it only becomes savings if the company cuts an expense or uses that time on something you can verify.

exemplo.texto: Today: 30 h until the invoice and 21 min of people time (median of the 5 cases, hypothesis); about 9% sent back ("about 15 a week" ÷ 168, stated, hypothesis). Count in the app and in the ERP for four weeks before version 2.0.

passos.sub: where, by when, without making what worse
texto: A goal is a value and a deadline, decided by whoever answers for the process, looking at the baseline and not at wishful thinking. Revise the goal when the observed baseline arrives: it may show the hypothesis was far off.
The guardrail protects what cannot get worse. If the goal is speed, the guardrail is error: a discount outside the policy, a wrong invoice, a complaint.

exemplo.texto: Goals for 8 weeks after version 2.0: median until the invoice of 24 h or less; returns of 3% or less; people minutes per order under 15. Guardrail: zero orders with a discount outside the policy.

Data from the lab's indicadores.json (fictional). The dashboard has no week before 01/07, when the agent came in: there is nothing to compare with.

• A count without a denominator. "15 returned" in a week of 100 orders is very different from in a week of 300.
  • Average time. One stuck case pulls the average up. Use the median and p95.
  • A hypothesis without a date. Every hypothesis says when it becomes observed.
  • Different periods. Comparing four year-end weeks with four weeks in February does not measure the redesign.
  • Freed-up time sold as savings. It only becomes savings with a reduced expense or a verified use.

secoes.sub: Fix Horizonte's dashboard; then measure your own process before changing it.
secoes.fonte: Lab piece: indicator dashboard (F11, fictional study company).

exercicios.texto: Open the dashboard in the lab. Calculate orders ÷ conversations for the first and the last week. Then write the three indicator sheets for the process from the order to the invoice, plus the guardrail. Finish with a three-sentence message to Carlos explaining why "goes up" does not answer whether the agent helped.
exercicios.pronto: both conversions are calculated, the 3 sheets have numerator, denominator, period, source, today's value marked as observed or hypothesis (with a date to become observed), goal and deadline, there is 1 guardrail with a limit, and the message to Carlos has 3 sentences.

exercicios.texto: Write the three indicator sheets for your process and start the baseline chart. Don't change anything in the process during the four weeks; if something changes, write it in the notes column.
exercicios.pronto: the 3 sheets are written with today's value as observed or hypothesis, and the chart has 4 weeks filled in with each week's denominator and the process owner's signature.

secoes.sub: 5 questions. The explanation appears after your attempt.

perguntas.p: The agent's conversations went from 702 to 901 a week. What does that prove?
opcoes: That the agent improved sales, since orders also went up
Nothing on its own: the before is missing and the denominator is missing; conversion fell
That the agent paid for itself, because it serves more people at the same cost
perguntas.explica: Volume can rise because of the time of year, a discount, or because the agent talks more per order. Conversion went from 20.1% to 18.6%, and "paid for itself" requires cost and the before. Without a baseline, the question "did it help?" stays a guess.

perguntas.p: Which of these is a complete indicator?
opcoes: Returned ÷ arrived at billing, per week, counted in the ERP
Orders returned by billing, counted in the ERP every week
Percentage of customers satisfied with the delivery, via the button
perguntas.explica: Numerator, denominator, period, and source. Counting returns every week still has no denominator: the number goes up and down with volume. Satisfaction via the button measures something else, with about 6% response.

perguntas.p: Finance says that "about 15 a week come back". How does this value go on the sheet?
opcoes: As observed, because finance sees all the orders
Leave it blank until the four-week count is finished
As a stated hypothesis, with the date it becomes observed
perguntas.explica: Stated is a valuable clue, but it is not a measurement, and leaving it blank loses the clue. Marking it as a hypothesis, with a date, protects the before-and-after comparison.

perguntas.p: Why use the median, not the average, for time to invoice?
opcoes: Because a few stuck cases pull the average up and hide the normal
Because the median always gives a lower number and an easier target
Because the average only works when there are more than a hundred cases in the week
perguntas.explica: In the five cases, the 75-hour order pulls the average up to about 40 hours; the median stays at 30. Median for the normal, p95 for the typical worst case. It is not to make the target easier: it is to avoid hiding the normal.

perguntas.p: The redesign freed up 20 hours of people's time per week. What can you tell the owner?
opcoes: That the company saved 20 hours of salary per week
That it freed up an estimated 20 hours, which are not yet savings
That the project's return is guaranteed starting next month
perguntas.explica: Freed-up capacity is not money in the bank. Any return is an estimate, with uncertainty, until the company cuts an expense or uses the time on something you can verify.

itens.texto: Without the before and without a denominator, "goes up" proves nothing.
Observed over four counted weeks, or a dated hypothesis.
Value and deadline, without worsening what cannot get worse.
